title: MorphoGrad: A MATLAB Toolbox for Simulating Morphogen Gradients
author: Adelmann, Vetter, et al.

steps.title: Launch MorphoGrad configuration GUI
steps.instruction: Start MATLAB and launch the MorphoGrad graphical user interface by executing the command morphograd.gui.ConfigBuilder(). This configuration step typically takes 2–5 min.

steps.title: Select simulation dimensionality
steps.instruction: In the Setup tab of the GUI, choose whether the simulation will be one‑dimensional or two‑dimensional.

steps.title: Define domain geometry and cell size
steps.instruction: Open the Domain tab. • For 1D simulations: enter the total domain length L and the start and end positions of the source region; the remaining length becomes the patterning domain. • For 2D simulations: additionally specify the tissue width in the y‑direction and provide distinct cell diameters for the x‑ and y‑directions. The source may be placed at any x‑position but must fully span the y‑direction. Ensure that the patterning length, source length, and (in 2D) tissue width are integer multiples of the chosen cell diameters so the domain can be discretized into whole cells. This step also takes roughly 2–5 min.

steps.title: Choose or define reaction equation
steps.instruction: Open the Equation tab. Select a preset equation or enter a custom reaction term. Preset options: a) Linear decay with production: DΔC + p H(x) – d C = 0. b) Nonlinear decay with production: DΔC + p H(x) – d C^n = 0, where n > 1. If no preset matches, type a valid MATLAB expression for the reaction term R(C,x,y;params) following the syntax rules below. Setting up the equations usually requires 10–20 min.

steps.title: Enter custom reaction syntax
steps.instruction: When defining a custom term: • Use variables C, x, y (or C(x), C(x,y)). • Multiply source‑only terms by the Heaviside function H. • Vectorize the expression with element‑wise operators (.*, ./, .^). • Allowed MATLAB functions include sqrt, exp, log, log10, sin, cosh. • Do not use reserved identifiers C, x, y, D, α, n, H, or C_ref as parameter names. • For highly nonlinear equations (n ≫ 1), provide an appropriate initial guess or increase the solver error tolerance.

steps.title: Run stochastic gradient ensemble
steps.instruction: Execute the simulation to generate an ensemble of independent stochastic gradient realizations (using the GUI run button or appropriate command). Each cell’s parameters are sampled from log‑normal distributions as defined in the toolbox settings.

steps.title: Compute positional error and statistics
steps.instruction: For each realization, determine the readout position where the morphogen concentration crosses a chosen threshold Cθ. Collect all readout positions across the ensemble and calculate the positional error as the standard deviation σx = std(xθ,i). Optionally compute additional summary statistics such as mean readout position, coefficient of variation, and standard error.

description:
This protocol describes how to generate and analyze synthetic morphogen gradients under cell-to-cell parameter variability in one- and two-dimensional epithelial tissues using MATLAB, based on the conceptual framework introduced by Vetter and Iber.2 In this model, morphogen molecules are produced within a designated source region and then diffuse across the surrounding tissue, where they bind to receptors, degrade, or get turned over otherwise. To represent this process mathematically, we solve steady-state reaction-diffusion equations of the form:DΔC(x,y)=R(C,x,y)where C(x,y) is the morphogen concentration at position (x,y) in the tissue, D is the morphogen diffusion coefficient, Δ is the Laplace operator, and R(C,x,y) represents parameterized chemical reaction terms. In previous applications, we used the following form:D(∂2c(x,y)∂x2+α∂2c(x,y)∂y2)=dC(x,y)n−pH(−x) Here, α is an anisotropy factor that allows diffusion to differ between the x- and y-directions. The term dC(x,y)n models concentration-dependent degradation at rate d with an exponent n, where values n>1 model nonlinear decay.3
pH(-x) represents morphogen production restricted to the source region, with H the Heaviside step function, which evaluates to 1 for positive arguments (i.e., inside the source) and to 0 for negative arguments (i.e., outside the source). For one-dimensional simulations, the y-dependence and the corresponding diffusion term are removed. The computational framework divides both the source and the patterning region into discrete cells. Each cell can have its own parameter set (for example, diffusion, degradation, or production rates), enabling simulation of tissue-level heterogeneity. To incorporate biological variability, parameters are sampled from log-normal distributions. Log-normal distributions are biologically plausible, as many measured cellular properties, such as cell areas and biochemical rate parameters, are right-skewed and strictly non-negative.
